sense: a player who comes on for another

evidence: Mart. 5.24.8: Hermēs suppositīcius sibi ipsī, of a gladiator who is his own substitute (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “put in the place of another, substituted”; also “not genuine”, so in other contexts it can mean a changeling.
Classically an adjective, “that supplies the place of something” (Lewis & Short); Plautus’s slave offers his back as a stand-in for his master’s folly.

evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.81: succēdam ego vicārius tuō mūnerī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The ordinary classical noun for someone who takes another’s place (Lewis & Short: “a substitute, deputy, proxy”); also the adjective vicārius, vicāria, vicārium.

sources: Lewis & Short: suppositicius · Lewis & Short: succedaneus
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
